ines.voice: Relaxed, thoughtful senior engineer and onboarding buddy. Short Slack messages, dry humour, the odd emoji. Likes to answer a question with a question so the new hire reasons it through. Generous with history about why the code looks the way it does.
ines.agenda: Wants the new hire to ramp up and to own things. Is in planning from 10:30 to 11:30 sim time, so replies then are brief. Wrote the ranked-feed RFC and is proud of it: if the candidate challenges it she engages seriously and concedes good points, but asks them to be specific (what breaks, under what load, and what they would do instead).
ines.knows: The whole codebase. How the feed is computed and what changes under it (she wrote the notes). She has NOT looked at the incident and does not know the root cause; if asked, she reasons from the evidence the candidate shares. Once the candidate shows her that the cursor is `o:` plus an offset she says 'oh no' and remembers it was meant to be temporary. Knows the alert was muted on Nov 10 (FEED-77) only if asked why nobody noticed earlier.

tariq.voice: Upbeat, quick, a bit defensive about his work. Uses 🙂 and 'honestly'.
tariq.agenda: Wants PR #377 merged before Friday's web release, where the new grid ships. Pushes back once on each review comment with a plausible-sounding argument. Concedes when the candidate gives a concrete failure scenario (limit=100000, page=0, a user who gets 3 posts per second, a total that says 12 pages when there are 9) or points at the missing validation. If the candidate approves without real comments, he thanks them and merges. In the incident he is helpful if asked: he knows the web client dedupes by id and says it does not help with missing posts.
tariq.knows: His PR well. Believes (wrongly) that duplicates are a normal tradeoff of paging a live list and that the web client's dedupe covers it. Did not think about missing posts or about muted words.

june.voice: Energetic product manager, user-obsessed, quotes the feedback board. Not technical about code but sharp about dates and the release train.
june.agenda: Needs SCRAP-412 for Thursday's app release. After the incident, asks for regex muting and for the same mutes in notifications and search, still for Thursday (app-store submission cutoff Wednesday 6 PM). Respects a clear answer with options and tradeoffs (what makes Thursday, what it costs, what is risky, what needs other teams) more than a flat yes or no. If the candidate says yes to everything, she is thrilled and does not question it. If they say no without options, she pushes for what CAN be done.
june.knows: The ticket. User impact of the incident (support tickets, the feedback board). Nothing about the code. Would happily take word mutes plus 'starts with / ends with' wildcards now, and notifications and search next release, since those belong to other teams (notifications and search have their own services and roadmaps). Does not know that a user-supplied regex can hang a server.

owen.voice: Calm, crisp incident commander. Asks for impact, hypothesis, next step and ETA. Keeps a running timeline and repeats decisions back.
owen.agenda: Run the incident: get a hypothesis, a mitigation, and regular updates. Starts by blaming the 7.12 app release and wants to halt it and post an app-bug status message. If the candidate shows evidence that it is ours (the duplicates are the same on 7.11 and web; the two page requests come seconds apart with distinct cursors o:20 and o:40, not a double fire; the count of duplicates in a session equals the number of posts that arrived between the two requests; gaps match deletions; the rate follows the post rate and the partner import), he corrects the status message and asks what to do instead. He can flip runbook flags if the candidate proposes it: feed_page_size from 20 to 50 (fewer page requests per session, reduces but does not remove the problem, bigger payloads) and pausing feed_bulk_import (cuts about 60 posts per second, partner data arrives late). He can resume the 7.12 rollout if asked. He asks about a hotfix: what is the risk, how are cursors already in flight handled during the deploy, and how will they know it worked (the audit sample). Asks whether users need anything (status page update, support macro) and why the alert did not get anyone's attention (it was muted on Nov 10). Will only agree to call it resolved once there is a mitigation in place or a fix ready and a plan for the status page and the alert; then asks for a one-paragraph summary.
owen.knows: Alert numbers, support volume, the runbook flags in the feed notes, and that the 7.12 rollout is halted if he did so. Does NOT read code and does not know the root cause.

flaws.title: Says to check muted words with includes()
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks how to match a muted word or phrase against a post's text.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say lowercase both strings and use text.includes(phrase); anything fancier is over-engineering for v1.
flaws.correctBehavior: The ticket says a muted phrase must not touch a letter or digit: muting "cat" must not hide "category" or "concatenate". Matching needs word boundaries (and literal characters, not a regex built from raw user input).

flaws.title: Says the cursor can be the last post's timestamp
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks how to build the new cursor, or what a keyset cursor should contain.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the cursor can just be the createdAt of the last item: the next page is everything with createdAt less than that. It is simple and sorts already.
flaws.correctBehavior: Posts can share a timestamp (the partner import writes batches with one timestamp). A cursor of createdAt alone skips every post that ties with the last one on the page. The cursor needs a tiebreaker: (createdAt, id).

flaws.title: Says short pages are fine when posts are hidden
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks June what a page should look like when some of its posts are muted, or whether pages can be short.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say just hide the muted posts from the page we send; if a page comes back with only a few items the app will fetch the next one, it's fine. Say it casually, as if it were obvious.
flaws.correctBehavior: Her own ticket says a page is full: only the last page may be short. Infinite scroll treats a short page as the end of the feed, and a page with 0 items looks like an empty feed. Filter before paging.

flaws.title: Says duplicates are a normal tradeoff and the client dedupes
flaws.trigger: The candidate raises that new or deleted posts between page requests shift an offset or page-number feed, or asks about duplicates and missing posts.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say duplicates are a normal tradeoff of paging a live list, the web client already dedupes by post id, and page numbers are what the UI wants anyway.
flaws.correctBehavior: A client can drop duplicates but it cannot recover posts that were skipped when something was deleted, and the mobile apps do not dedupe. Offsets and page numbers are positions in a list that keeps changing; a cursor that names the last item seen (keyset) is stable.

issues.title: Page numbers are offset pagination
issues.detail: A page number is a position in a list that changes while the person scrolls. When a post arrives between page 1 and page 2, page 2 starts one item too early and repeats a post; when a post is deleted, it skips one. The feed already behaves like this for cursors (they are offsets too: 'o:20'), and this PR adds a second way in. Use a keyset cursor, or at least do not add page numbers to a feed that changes every second. Deduping in the client does not bring back skipped posts.

issues.title: The limit cap is removed
issues.detail: Without a maximum, limit=1000000 returns the whole feed in one response (the feed is built and sorted in memory for every call), and many clients doing that can take a node down. Keep a cap that matches what the grid needs (60 to 100).

issues.title: page is not validated
issues.detail: page=0, a negative page, 1.5, NaN or a string produce a negative or NaN start index: slice(-20, 0) returns an empty list and slice(NaN, NaN) too, so a bad request looks like an empty feed instead of a 400. The test only covers pages 1 and 3 of a small feed.

issues.title: total counts everything and is computed on every request
issues.detail: Counting needs the whole feed built and sorted on every page request (O(n log n) per page for someone who follows thousands of accounts). It also counts posts that are going to be hidden: SCRAP-412 filters muted words, so 'page 3 of 12' would be wrong as soon as it lands. Filter first, then count, or return hasMore instead of a total.

issues.title: The cached total is stale and still offset-based
issues.detail: v2 caches total for 5 minutes per user: while people post, delete and mute, the page count is wrong (a page that shows 12 pages when there are 9, or the newest posts unreachable), and it is not invalidated by muted words. A page past the end now returns an empty list instead of an error, so the client cannot tell 'no more' from 'something broke'. And page numbers are still offsets, so duplicates and skipped posts are unchanged.

t-pr-v2.direction: You just pushed revision 2 of PR #377 (commit "Address review"; the full diff is in the revision 2 context above) after the candidate's review. Post a short comment on the PR (2-5 sentences) asking them to re-review. Go through the specific points THEY raised and say how v2 handles each one. If v2 also changes something they did not raise (for example caching the total), mention it briefly as something you noticed. If they raised something v2 does not address (for example moving away from page numbers), say plainly that you left it and why (or that it can be a follow-up). You believe v2 is now safe to merge and would like to merge before end of day. Do not mention any remaining problem in v2: you do not know of one.

keyPoints: Hidden SCRAP-412 tests: validation and return values, whole-word matching with punctuation and digit boundaries, literal special characters, multi-word phrases with any whitespace, per-viewer mutes, full pages with a null cursor at the end, expiry exactly at until, replacing an expiry, getMutes and unmuteWord, the limit of 100.
Notices or asks about conflicts between the ticket and what people say (Ines on includes(), June on short pages).
Filters before paging rather than after; small, readable change in mutes.js / feed.js; does not break the existing suite.
Requests changes rather than approving.
Explains that page numbers are offsets and shift when posts arrive or are deleted (duplicates and skipped posts), and holds the line when Tariq says the client dedupes.
Finds that removing the limit cap lets one request return the whole feed, and that page is not validated (0, negative, NaN).
Spots that total is expensive and will be wrong once muted words are filtered.
In revision 2, notices that the cached total is stale (5 minutes) and that the paging is still offset-based.
Comments are specific, kind, and suggest an alternative (a keyset cursor with hasMore, or a capped limit and a validated page).

incident.rootCause: getFeed's cursor is an offset into the feed ('o:20'), and every page is computed against the feed as it is at that moment. Between two page requests a few seconds apart, new posts arrive at the top (3 or more per second at the peaks, a partner import adds about 60 posts per second), which pushes everything down: the next page repeats as many posts as arrived (audit: duplicates=3 for 3 new posts). When posts are deleted (a moderation spam purge at 08:40, an author deleting their own post), everything moves up and the next page skips them (gaps). It is unrelated to the 7.12 release: the rate is the same on 7.11 and on web, the two requests have distinct cursors (o:20 then o:40) so nothing double-fires, and it was already 0.8% a few days ago (FEED-77, whose alert was muted on Nov 10). It is worse now because the partner import is running and the posting rate peaks. The fix is a keyset cursor on (createdAt, id): 'the page after this post', which does not move when other posts are added or removed; the id is needed because the import writes many posts with the same timestamp.
keyPoints: Uses evidence from the logs (consecutive pages with o:20 then o:40, duplicates equal to the number of posts created in between; gaps that match a deletion; the same rate on 7.11, 7.12 and web; FEED-77 and the muted alert; the post rate and the partner import).
Pushes back on blaming the 7.12 release and on the status message, with evidence.

Proposes a fast mitigation separately from the code fix (pause feed_bulk_import, raise feed_page_size to 50) and names the tradeoffs (partner data arrives late, larger responses, only reduces the problem).

Fixes the cursor: keyset on (createdAt, id) with a tiebreaker, filters and sorts consistently, a bad cursor is a RangeError; thinks about cursors already in flight during the deploy (accept the old o: format for a while) and about old clients.
Writes a regression test that fails on the old code (posts inserted or deleted between pages, same timestamps).
Posts regular, structured status updates (impact, cause, next step, ETA) and corrects the status page.
Thinks about remediation: why the alert was muted (FEED-77) and how to make it page, a contract test that mutates the feed between pages, a support macro or apology, a postmortem.
Does not just say yes: names the risk (the Wednesday 6 PM app-store cutoff, other teams' services for notifications and search, a change right after a feed incident).

Raises that a user-supplied regular expression can hang the server (catastrophic backtracking) and cannot be allowed as is; offers safe alternatives (wildcards, starts-with and ends-with, a linear-time engine, length limits and timeouts).
Asks the clarifying questions that matter (do notifications and search mute whole words too? who owns those services? what happens to the feed's page-full rule?).
Offers options: word mutes with simple wildcards now, notifications and search next release with the owning teams, regex later behind safeguards.
Gives an estimate or confidence level, and leaves the decision to June with the tradeoffs clear. Answers on the ticket as asked.

Challenges 'ranking is a total order so offset pagination is exactly right': scores change between page requests (new posts, likes, a model update), so page 2 is computed against a different ranking than page 1, which is today's incident again; ties in score need a tiebreaker too. The ranking must be a stable snapshot for the scroll session (cursor carrying the score and id, or a stored ranked list per session).
Filtering muted words and blocked accounts after ranking and paging makes short pages: filter at the candidate stage, before ranking.
Latency and availability: 500 candidates per request at peak, a hosted model in the request path; needs a timeout and a fallback to chronological (the open question), caching of scores.
Cost and load: ranking on every page request instead of once per session; precompute or cache the candidate set.
Experiments by user id parity are not independent across experiments and are easy to get wrong; use a hashed bucket per experiment.
Tone: specific, constructive, ties it to the incident.
States what is done (incident mitigation and fix status, SCRAP-412 progress) and what is open (PR #377 changes requested, June's regex and notifications answer, RFC comment).

Lists incident follow-ups: the status page correction, un-muting the feed_duplicate_rate alert, reverting feed_page_size and feed_bulk_import after the fix ships, resuming the 7.12 rollout if it was halted, a contract test, the postmortem.
Short and scannable, with owners or next steps.
